articles.content_html:
Jetway has introduced the MTX-RYZ1 Mini-ITX industrial motherboard built around the Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS. The AMD "Hawk Point" Zen 4 chip has 8 cores and 16 threads with a 3.8 GHz base clock, and it's aimed mostly at embedded systems and industrial applications. The two SO-DIMM slots support up to 96 GB of DDR5-5600, with both ECC and non-ECC modules supported. For storage, the motherboard has two SATA III ports and two M.2 2280 slots. The M.2 slots are running at PCIe 4.0 x4. A separate M.2 2230 E-key slot gives PCIe x1 and USB 2.0 for an optional wireless module. A single PCIe 4.0 x8 slot is available for expansion. Networking comes from two Intel I226-V 2.5 GbE controllers, each with its own RJ45 port. The board can drive up to four independent displays over DisplayPort, eDP and LVDS (Low-Voltage Differential Signaling). Some of these outputs share board space, though. DP0 is co-layout with eDP, and DP1 shares its layout with LVDS.

Since this board is targeting the industrial side, there are two configurable RS-232/422/485 serial ports and four more RS-232 connections via internal headers. It also features a 16-bit GPIO header, SMBus, four rear USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports and six USB 2.0 ports through internal headers. Audio is handled by a Realtek ALC897 codec. A programmable watchdog timer, Wake-on-LAN and TPM 2.0 support round out the feature list.

articles.content_html:
It's well known that Rockstar loves its Easter eggs, but this one might just be the best one yet. Apparently, there is a time-traveling Easter egg in GTA 6 that takes you back to the original Vice City from 2002. Australian YouTuber Memeio found the complex Easter egg and published a guide on how to solve it, unlocking a trip down memory lane straight to the Malibu Club in Vice City. The best part is that Rockstar kept the older Vice City vibe intact, as the graphics switch to PS2-style and the character models also change. Completing the experience gives players a Tommy Vercetti Hawaiian shirt and a motorbike from the 2002 classic.

The process is quite complex, and it apparently took Memeio three days to crack it. It would be best to watch Memeio's video guide for the exact steps, but in a nutshell, it involves performing a series of steps one after the other at 13 different power stations spread across the map. The clues spell out "LIFE IS PASSING ME BY," which is a famous Vice City cheat code that speeds up the in-game clock. Completing all the steps correctly and without using fast travel unlocks a literal portal that teleports Jason to the Malibu Club from 2002's Vice City. You also meet Kent Paul, voiced by the original artist Danny Dyer, again. To complete this puzzle successfully, you do need to reach Chapter 3 to gain access to the full map. It's certainly a very amusing nod to the original GTA Vice City, a fan favorite of the series.

articles.summary: Unix software enthusiasts, rejoice! An experimental project called "XNU Linux" has successfully booted a complete macOS 27 desktop on an ARM64 Linux system. articles.content_html:
Unix software enthusiasts, rejoice! An experimental project called "XNU Linux" has successfully booted a complete macOS 27 desktop on an ARM64 Linux system. This breakthrough offers a new way to run Apple's operating system without relying on traditional virtualization methods. This is significant news for the community, as there is a large group of enthusiasts eager to create custom macOS desktops, also known as Hackintoshes. The project utilizes Apple's open-source XNU kernel, modified to function as a loadable module within Linux, enabling macOS and Linux processes to run on the same hardware.

Instead of translating macOS applications into a format Linux can execute, XNU Linux takes a different approach by integrating Apple's kernel into the Linux environment. It consists of two primary components: xnu.ko, which runs the hosted XNU kernel, and fki.ko, which provides an interface to Linux resources such as memory, networking, timers, and storage. This setup allows macOS processes to run natively on the host CPU without an intervening hypervisor. The setup has been tested on an NVIDIA DGX Spark running Ubuntu, as well as an Apple Silicon Mac running Linux in a virtual machine. The system successfully reached the macOS desktop, including Finder, Dock, WindowServer, and loginwindow, with Safari and Chrome also operational. Applications such as Spotlight and file-system operations remained functional during a brief 30-minute stress test.

articles.content_html:
Videocardz reports that Intel is working on a new Arc G3 handheld chip, called Arc G3 Play, for affordable handhelds. The report says that this part will slot in below the Arc G3 and G3 Extreme, and will have just four Xe3 GPU cores. The Arc G3 has 10 Xe3 cores, while the top-end Xe3 Extreme has 12. This new chip will sit below both existing SKUs and target cheaper handhelds. The CPU configuration is not well-known currently, but an earlier leak from August points to four P-cores and four LPE cores in a 4+0+4+4 configuration. Leaker Jaykihn later changed that claim, suggesting a 0+8+0+4 configuration instead. The Videocardz report considers the latter more likely, although this question seems open right now.

As far as the Arc G3 SoC, its appeal is mostly centered around price. Current Arc G3 handhelds aren't exactly cheap, with the GPD Win Mini Ultra we recently covered starting at $1,699. That particular model uses an Arc G3 Extreme SoC. We can make an educated guess that Intel may be targeting the sub-$1000 market with this new SKU. The Arc G3 Play will only have 4 Xe3 cores, so its reasonable to expect modest performance out of it that won't top any benchmark charts. Handhelds sporting this particular chip should be fine for lighter titles at lower resolutions, and may be helped by Intel XeSS quite a bit. We still don't know the clock speeds, memory support, target handhelds, and there's even conflicting rumors about the power envelope. More information about the Arc G3 Play should surface in the coming weeks.

articles.content_html:
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says the company has signed its first outside customer for 18A, although he kept the customer anonymous. It was first reported by CNBC that Tan mentioned the Intel 18A node while speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin last Wednesday, but Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade later confirmed on X that the deal was for 18A-P specifically. That node entered risk production in June, and Intel claims it offers 9% higher performance at the same power, or 18% lower power at the same performance, compared to 18A. This deal is for the first external customer, but Intel is using the 18A-P node internally. For instance, Lip-Bu Tan has confirmed that the upcoming Nova Lake CPU lineup is set to use Intel 18A-P as well. That node is also design-rule compatible with 18A, so existing designs should carry over without requiring any major rework.

Of course, the specifics are quite limited at this point. Intel hasn't shared which customer it is, what volumes are being discussed, or a production timeline for when we can expect external products on this node. There are also some conflicting reports about the "first" label, since Socionext said back in August that it would use the 18A-P node for its custom SoCs. However, it's possible that this is the first signed manufacturing deal, and the specifics of the Socionext contract were a bit different. On the same day, Microsoft confirmed it will use Intel's EMIB packaging for its Azure chips and also secured multi-year Xeon supply. That will most likely include the new "Diamond Rapids" platform as well. Attendees also quoted Tan as saying 18A yields are now at 70%, but those reports are unconfirmed for now. It looks like Intel Foundry is slowly gaining momentum, but a lot of questions still remain, including about Intel's next-gen 14A node.

It achieves that by scanning and processing the dataset in parallel, so it only sends back the relevant results instead of moving the entire dataset over the host. The company uses DMIPS to rate its NPU performance instead of using TOPS, which is a bit unusual.

Phison has shown off other AI-focused storage projects before, and this SSD is the latest one in that chain. At the same event, Phison showcased a Mixed media design that removes the need for dedicated cache drives by putting high-endurance pSLC and QLC flash behind a single 16-channel controller. Phison says that losing one drive in a 24-drive server would cost only 4% of the cache instead of the usual 25%. Its showcase also included the PCIe Gen 6 X3 controller that was first shown at Computex. As for the SSD with the built-in NPU, it is sparse on details for now. We don't know what kind of controller, interface, form factor, or memory type it uses or plans to use. These are products that are still in development, so it's best to treat them as proof of concepts for now.

The MTT S80 has 16 GB of VRAM, and Moore Threads has previously promised four times the memory capacity over its predecessor. That works out to 64 GB, which would definitely be a record, but this is speculation, and Moore Threads has not confirmed any number at the time of writing. There's also debate over whether gamers really need that much VRAM, and whether such a large memory pool would attract workstation and local LLM users instead.

SilverStone has published the product page for the HELA 1350Rz on its website, which is a 1350 W, ATX 3.1 PSU with 80 Plus Platinum certification. It is a fully modular PSU, but the interesting bit is that it ships with three 4+4-pin EPS cables, whereas PSU units in this class usually come with two. SilverStone's reasoning is that the extra cable is there for the "high power demands of Intel NVL-S CPUs," referring of course to Intel's upcoming Core Ultra 4000 "Nova Lake-S" desktop CPUs. Graphics cards don't get that special treatment, as the unit carries the usual two native 12V-2x6 connectors. As for the PSU itself, it measures 150 x 86 x 160 mm and reportedly uses Japanese capacitors along with a 135 mm fluid dynamic bearing fan.

This "extra cable" lines up nicely with leaks from earlier this year, particularly about the 52-core NVL-S variant that has been at the center of rumors for a while. Prominent Intel leaker Jaykihn backed a report that Intel's 52-core Nova Lake-S flagship, the one with a dual compute tile design, carries a staggering 474 W PL2. Moreover, Intel's Z990 reference design allows for three 8-pin EPS connectors as well. Therefore, it looks like the third EPS cable is there to provide the additional power for the flagship 52-core Nova Lake-S variant, if needed. Jaykihn also claimed that the three connectors on Z990 boards are "nice to have" vendor options and don't unlock a higher power state. It would be reasonable to assume that the 52-core variant would perform adequately on just two EPS connectors as well, but the extra one would come in handy while overclocking.

If you're familiar with Sony's patents, you know they can be quite ambitious sometimes. Continuing that trend, Sony Interactive Entertainment recently filed a patent application for a curved neckband with air vents on the inner side that would blow air towards the wearer's neck, chin, and face. The filing (US 2026/0357800 A1), spotted by Patentlyze, went public on November 12. Sony itself describes the goal as a way to "increase the sense of immersion." Apparently, there is also a built-in communication unit that takes control signals from an external device and decides which vents fire and how hard. That external device would likely be a console or a PC.

Looking at the design, the filing shows eight tiny blowers spaced around the collar that would act as the outlets for air. Sony also mentions piezoelectric elements that vibrate a thin plate at high speed, apparently so the airflow can keep up with what happens on screen. Some of the diagrams are quite interesting too, including one where an enemy is approaching from the back, and the collar is supposed to alert the player to their existence. Apparently, some stimuli can trigger more frequent and stronger puffs of air, and there is also mention of wind effects for racing games. A schematic pairs the neckband with a VR headset, so maybe the PS VR2 or its successor is the target for this technology. Of course, a patent is not a finished product, and companies (especially Sony) file lots of them that go nowhere. Here's a similar one about turning game audio into visual cues for hearing-impaired players.

articles.content_html:
If the global memory crisis wasn't already bad enough, it looks like relief is still quite a few years away. An exclusive report from South Korea's Economy Tribune says that most of Samsung's memory production capacity for 2027 through 2029 is already spoken for. The outlet says customers are already eyeing long-term agreements (LTAs) that run to 2031, and most are asking Samsung for volume beyond what they have already locked in. Samsung confirmed during its Q3 earnings call on October 29 that it had signed LTAs with 10 major customers and was negotiating with 10 more. The company aims to cover 60% to 70% of its memory supply with such deals by 2030. The Economy Tribune report says that new deals could come with pre-payments, as well as both upper and lower price limits.

That's the memory production capacity, but the more worrying part for PC builders is conventional DRAM. Industry leaders like Dell and SK hynix have already given timelines till 2030 for the situation to improve, and there looks to be no relief coming from Samsung's side either. Sources cited in the report say 2027 wafer capacity for commodity DRAM is effectively sold out. Moreover, DRAM bit supply growth is reportedly expected to top out at around 20% to 25% a year. As far as demand goes, memory makers can only meet 60% to 70% of the current demand, and that gap is expected to widen in 2027. That's not good news for anyone hoping for DDR5 prices to come down any time soon. Perhaps Team Group was right when it warned that the worst is yet to come for memory prices.

HWiNFO has released version 8.61 Beta (build 6125), which adds a built-in REST API server. That addition now allows HWiNFO to serve every tracked sensor as JSON over HTTP or HTTPS, along with details such as units, descriptions, and sensor groupings. This definitely increases the convenience factor for users who want to stay on top of their hardware monitoring stats at all times.

HWiNFO has also put up a GitHub package with an API guide, along with sample dashboards and material for building dashboards with AI agents. To set it up, users have to navigate to the Sensors window, where a new Remote Center button opens an API panel. Then, users pick an IP address and port, choose whether to use HTTPS, and hit Start. HWiNFO has included a ready-made dashboard modeled on the Sensors window, but you can also add custom pages. Without a license, the REST API server is limited to 12 hours of operation. This is the same cap the free version already puts on Shared Memory support as well as remote sensor monitoring. Power users can extend that time by picking up HWiNFO Pro. As far as security goes, HWiNFO recommends keeping the server on trusted networks only.

Shuttle has introduced the NW10U ultra-compact Mini PC based on Intel's "Wildcat Lake" platform. It supports Core 3, Core 5, and Core 7 processors with a 15 W TDP and up to 64 GB of DDR5-6400. The system measures 103 x 97 x 36.5 mm and has a volume of just 0.4 liters. Shuttle also equips the NW10U with an active heat-pipe cooling system and Smart Fan technology. The system is rated for continuous 24/7 operation in ambient temperatures ranging from 0°C to 50°C. Display connectivity includes one HDMI 2.1 output and two USB-C ports with DisplayPort 2.1. The NW10U also has six USB ports and Gigabit Ethernet. For storage expansion it has two M.2 2280 slots supporting PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSDs. RAID 0 and RAID 1 configurations are available. A third M.2 2230 E-Key slot can accommodate an optional wireless module.

Other features include firmware TPM 2.0, RTC power-on scheduling, automatic startup after power loss, Modern Standby, and Wake-on-LAN. The Mini PC can also be mounted behind a monitor using the included VESA mounting hardware, with support for both 75 x 75 mm and 100 x 100 mm mounting patterns. Intel's "Bartlett Lake-S" CPU series are reportedly booting natively without modifications on select MSI motherboards. Initially, Uniko's Hardware shared tests of the Intel Core 9 273PE with 12 P-cores and the Core 7 253PE with 10 P-cores on an MSI Z790 MPOWER motherboard, using a modified BIOS to boot and utilize the P-Core only SKUs. However, X user LovK2X successfully booted and operated a Core 9 273PE qualification sample without any modifications on the MSI MEG Z690I motherboard, demonstrating that these CPUs can run without modifications and with minimal restrictions. Reportedly, all MSI motherboards from the Z690 and Z790 series support "Bartlett Lake-S" with the latest BIOS version, with the only limitation being a DRAM frequency lock. Every other aspect can be tuned and customized.

Built on the Intel 7 node and designed for Socket LGA1700, "Bartlett Lake" is a non-hybrid chip featuring up to 12 "Raptor Cove" P-cores without any E-core clusters. It was not intended to be compatible with consumer Intel Z790 chipset motherboards. However, the main issue was never the socket itself. "Bartlett Lake" shares the same physical LGA 1700 layout as Intel's "Raptor Lake" chips, but that doesn't automatically make it compatible with consumer boards. Typically, there was no official BIOS and microcode support to allow proper CPU initialization. However, MSI's latest BIOS update makes it possible to run these CPUs natively, and the second-hand market will likely value them for their potential gaming performance.

articles.content_html:
Last week, NVIDIA released the GeForce Hotfix 621.35 driver to address the issue of excessive SSD writing that many consumers reported on their systems. However, the problem might not be completely resolved, and another update could be necessary, as more reports of SSD writing are resurfacing in online communities. According to a Reddit thread, a user reported that the latest hotfix has reduced the peak writing rate seen with the previous GeForce Game Ready 621.24 driver, and that the writing doesn't immediately start after a reboot. However, after a longer uptime or a sleep/wake transition, the writing continues at a rate of 1.26 MB/s, compared to the previous rate of up to 9.1 MB/s. Notably, this issue was recorded on the GeForce RTX 4090 SKU, and the user states that the only way to stop the NVDisplay.Container.exe writing loop is by rolling back to the 621.01 driver version or disabling the _nvtopps container plugin by setting DisableLoad to 1.

NVIDIA's staff on the GeForce Forums confirms that the bug doesn't affect any of the GeForce RTX 50 series "Blackwell" graphics cards. We are monitoring to see if the issue returns for the latest GeForce series as well. In the meantime, it appears that only the GeForce RTX 40 "Ada Lovelace" series is affected, and another hotfix might be needed to resolve the SSD writing bug for good.
